claims.text: A Pulumi blog post exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi", and it covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration from CDK to Pulumi.
AWS CDK tied infrastructure to AWS.
Multi-cloud was nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
SST was originally built on top of AWS CDK, which allowed developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
With CDK and CloudFormation, infrastructure code acts as a code generator producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources.
AWS CDK is AWS-only, whereas Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-prem.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python, whereas Pulumi supports any programming language.
Pulumi deployments are faster than AWS CDK deployments because of direct execution versus CloudFormation.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file while Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK supports only AWS Secrets Manager for secrets management, while Pulumi supports cross-cloud secrets.
Pulumi offers real-time debugging.
Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment instead of generating an intermediary format.

A Founding Engineer at SST said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
Pulumi Insights product page describes improved visibility and debugging capabilities.
Pulumi has built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components.
Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments.
Pulumi Cloud Deployments documentation exists at /docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies 'day one' tasks, documented in the AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
An on-demand Pulumi workshop titled 'Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS' exists at the given resources URL.
Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, whose components are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine while also bridging Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service called SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
SST is a framework for building modern full-stack applications on your own infrastructure.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` needs no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps its state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account, not in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the Ion-based rewrite of the SST framework.
`sst deploy` does not require CDK, CloudFormation, a Pulumi account, or Pulumi Cloud.
Nitric and Defang also run application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building their own diff, state, and provider layer.
SST's team is publicly associated with opencode, an AI coding agent.
The SST team has repeatedly stated, since the rewrite shipped, that SST is built on the Pulumi engine.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST can deploy applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST apps define infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST components, and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced the entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported architecture since.

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs ('What is SST') say: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin, in 'Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis', wrote that SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to SST's constructs.
Kiryl Anoshka, in 'SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion', wrote: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published package.json for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi` plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds and more, alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider.

The SST repository is at `anomalyco/sst` (formerly `sst/sst`), and platform/package.json lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.
The Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
Terraform-bridged providers, via Pulumi's Terraform bridge, translate each resource into cloud API calls.
SST components compile into Pulumi resource declarations, and `sst deploy` reads `sst.config.ts` and resolves SST's own components.
The Pulumi engine handles dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's provider ecosystem for the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API lets teams embed Pulumi programs inside their own tools, working the same embedded way.
The Pulumi provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.

The linked docs and blog pages exist: /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/, /blog/any-terraform-provider/, /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/, /docs/iac/concepts/pulumi-cloud/, /docs/iac/concepts/policy/, /docs/iac/concepts/components/, /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/, /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/.
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework whose docs state "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Official Nitric providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.
Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud, and its Pulumi provider is described as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`".
Nitric and Defang, like SST, expose a narrower, more opinionated interface to users while relying on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge.
Most SST users never write Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.
Resources without a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly in Pulumi inside an SST app and deployed as part of the same app.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads a week (796,291 for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
opencode is an open source AI coding agent that now has a larger GitHub star count than SST.
SST's team page credits the same team behind opencode.
SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine has not changed and its release cadence has not changed since the team's attention broadened to opencode.
SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state; its components use Terraform providers bridged through the Pulumi engine.

Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state, policy as code enables central guardrail enforcement, and components enable sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
SST does not expose cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across more than one application on its own.
Anyone who runs SST is running Pulumi's engine.
